title: Tracing SDK and Middleware: robust context propagation across async edges
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Background: Our tracing pipeline currently loses trace context across several async boundaries (background jobs, HTTP client retries, and cross-service pub/sub flows), causing lower trace completion rates in latency/error dashboards and making debugging production incidents harder. Goal: Implement SDK and middleware changes to propagate W3C Trace Context and lightweight baggage reliably across Node, Python, and Java runtimes; provide explicit middleware/instrumentation for common frameworks (Express, Fastify, aiohttp, grpc); and add automated tests + benchmarks so rollout is safe.
acceptance_criteria: W3C traceparent header is preserved end-to-end for HTTP sync flows for Node/Python/Java services in our staging workloads
Async boundaries: background workers and scheduled jobs attach parent trace IDs so traces complete instead of orphaning spans
End-to-end tests cover at least 3 failure modes (lost headers, retry with new connection, cross-thread handoff) with deterministic pass/fail
Instrumentation overhead measurable and within performance budget: <2% p50 latency increase and <5% p99 tokenized overhead on representative microservice benchmarks
Feature toggles and rollout plan exist (canary -> org-wide) with dashboards showing trace completion rate, trace drop rate, and span count per request
Docs updated with integration snippets for Express, Fastify, aiohttp, and Java gRPC interceptors + migration notes
design_notes: Decisions: 1) Use W3C Trace Context as the canonical propagation format and support legacy X-Trace-Id header for compatibility. 2) Integrate OpenTelemetry API for span creation but keep a thin Redwood wrapper API to avoid breaking changes. 3) For Node, use async_hooks with a fallback to CLS-hooked where async_hooks is restricted; for Python, rely on contextvars and explicit context injection for worker pools. 4) Keep baggage minimal (key whitelist) to avoid header bloat. Trade-offs: async_hooks gives best transparency but has edge cases with native modules—we'll gate on Node >= 18 and opt-out for older runtimes. For high-throughput services, prefer manual context passing in hot paths to avoid async context overhead. Rollback approach: feature flag to disable instrumentation globally and explicit env var to force legacy behavior.
implementation_plan:
Tasks:
- Build Redwood-tracing SDK adapters for Node, Python, Java (ENG-4927-A/B/C)
- Add middleware for Express/Fastify; interceptors for gRPC; instrument HTTP client libs (fetch, axios, requests)
- Implement context propagation helpers for worker frameworks (Bull, Celery, Sidekiq patterns)
- Add unit/e2e tests that simulate header stripping, retries, and background handoffs
- Microbenchmarks and load tests comparing current baseline vs new SDK on staging cluster
- Docs and migration guide; sample code for internal teams
- Rollout: internal canary (10% traffic) -> org beta -> global (toggle per service)
telemetry_test_plan: Create synthetic traces across service graph in staging: API gateway -> service A (HTTP) -> queued job -> worker -> datastore. Assertions: span tree intact, trace duration consistent, no orphaned spans. Add metrics: trace_completion_rate (ratio of traces with root->leaf), header_drop_rate, span_count_distribution, sdk_instrumentation_failure_count. Create a dataplane alert if trace_completion_rate drops >5% vs baseline.
performance_budget: Target overhead: p50 <2% increase, p99 <5% increase on representative CPU-bound and I/O-bound endpoints. Memory overhead: SDK resident memory <15MB per process for Node; Python <10MB. If budgets exceeded, revert to manual instrumentation fallback for affected services.
